 Creating a good survey is harder than it appears. A survey can look complete while still containing leading language, double-barrelled questions, unclear timeframes, sensitive questions without an opt-out, conflicting response options, or unnecessary requests for personal information. 

 These issues are often identified through manual reviews, long checklists, and repeated back-and-forth between researchers, product teams, and stakeholders. The process takes time, depends heavily on reviewer experience, and can still produce inconsistent results. 

 SurveyGuard was inspired by a simple question: 

 What if a person and an AI agent could review and improve a survey together inside the same live workspace? 

 Instead of requiring an agent to interpret buttons, scrape page content, or guess how the survey application works, SurveyGuard exposes clearly defined survey actions through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the survey, identify risks, explain findings, and perform approved actions while the person remains in control. 

 What SurveyGuard does
SurveyGuard is a WebMCP-enabled survey quality workspace that helps people and AI agents collaboratively review surveys before publication. 

 The current MVP allows users to: 

 Create, edit, and delete survey questions
Configure question types and response options
Validate survey questions against defined quality checks
Identify personally identifiable information
Detect leading or loaded wording
Flag potentially double-barrelled questions
Identify sensitive questions that may need a “Prefer not to answer” option
Detect unclear reference periods
Flag exclusive options such as “None of these” in multi-select questions
Review findings by severity
Apply recommended corrections
Monitor a dynamic survey-readiness score
Generate a concise survey-readiness report
Findings are organized into three levels: 

 Blocking: A high-risk issue that should be addressed before publication
Needs review: An issue requiring human judgment or revision
Suggestion: A non-blocking quality improvement
SurveyGuard uses fictional survey content in the demonstration and does not depend on private company data, confidential research, or customer information. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit
Survey review is not just a question-and-answer experience. It requires an agent to inspect structured survey content, understand validation results, modify specific questions, add response options, and confirm how those actions changed the survey. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent may have to infer this structure from the visual interface and navigate the application indirectly. That approach can be slow, fragile, and difficult to verify. 

 With WebMCP, SurveyGuard exposes narrow and intentional tools that describe exactly what an agent can do. The agent works with the same survey and application state that the user sees. 

 The MVP includes the following site tools: 

 get_survey_summary
list_questions
validate_survey
rewrite_question
add_prefer_not_to_answer
generate_readiness_report
For example, a user can ask an agent to: 

 Validate this survey, explain the highest-risk issue, and help me fix it. 

 The agent can call the validation tool, return structured findings, explain the most important issue, and then use an appropriate write tool after the user approves the change. 

 This creates a more reliable experience than asking the agent to guess how to manipulate the interface. 

 Human-agent collaboration
SurveyGuard is designed around human review rather than unattended automation. 

 The application separates inspection from modification: 

 The agent retrieves the current survey structure.
The agent runs structured validation.
The agent explains the identified issues.
The user reviews the recommendation.
An approved change is applied through a specific WebMCP tool.
The interface updates so the user can verify the result.
SurveyGuard recalculates the readiness score and remaining findings.
The agent provides speed and consistency, while the user maintains responsibility for context, judgment, and final approval. 

 This is particularly important in survey design because whether a question is appropriate can depend on the research objective, intended audience, jurisdiction, and sensitivity of the subject. 

 How I built it
SurveyGuard was built as a React-based web application with a responsive three-panel review experience: 

 A question list for navigating the survey
An editor for reviewing wording, question type, and response options
A validation panel for displaying findings and recommended actions
The validation engine evaluates each question using transparent, deterministic rules. Each finding includes: 

 A unique issue code
A severity level
A short title
An explanation
A recommended correction or action when appropriate
The interface calculates a survey-readiness score based on the number and severity of unresolved findings. The score updates as users edit questions or apply corrections. 

 WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool defines: 

 A specific name
A focused description
A narrow input schema
Required parameters
Read-only annotations where applicable
An execution handler connected to the survey’s existing application logic
The tools return structured results so an agent can understand what happened and communicate the result to the user. 

 The application also preserves a normal visual workflow for people and can display a preview state when WebMCP is not available in the current browser environment. 

 Challenges I faced
Designing useful tool boundaries
One challenge was deciding how much authority each tool should have. A single broad tool that could change the entire survey would be flexible, but it would also be harder to control and verify. 

 I chose narrower tools such as rewrite_question and add_prefer_not_to_answer. This makes each action easier for the agent to select, easier for the user to understand, and easier to test. 

 Separating blocking issues from recommendations
Not every survey-quality concern should prevent publication. Treating every finding as equally severe would create unnecessary friction and reduce trust in the validator. 

 To address this, SurveyGuard separates blocking issues, review items, and optional suggestions. 

 Keeping the human in control
A technically successful agent action is not necessarily the right research decision. SurveyGuard therefore treats agent recommendations as reviewable actions and clearly communicates that human approval is recommended before publication. 

 Managing shared application state
WebMCP tools and the visible interface need to operate on the same current survey. Tool outputs, question edits, validation results, and readiness scoring must remain consistent after every action. 

 The MVP connects tool execution to the same underlying state used by the visual interface so changes can be seen and verified immediately. 

 Working within a short build window
The challenge required prioritizing a focused, demonstrable workflow. Instead of attempting to build a complete survey-authoring platform, I concentrated on the core WebMCP experience: inspect, validate, explain, improve, and verify. 

 What I learned
Building SurveyGuard reinforced several important lessons: 

 Agent-native applications need explicit actions, not just an AI chat box.
